title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for undirected weighted Steiner Tree under worst-case polynomial running time. For the valid instances \(\mathcal I\) and the uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms \(\mathcal A\) defined below, put
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:
r\ge1\ \land\
\exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\
\mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\right]
\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=\inf\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}.
\]
Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. The expectation concerns output cost, not running time. No complexity assumption is part of the definition. The requested error is additive in this dimensionless approximation ratio.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,E,R,w)\) consists of a connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), a set of terminals \(R\subseteq[n]\) with \(2\le |R|\le n\), and nonnegative rational weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices; each pair occurs at most once. Connected means every two vertices are joined by a finite path. The whole graph, terminal list and all weights are explicitly given. There is no restriction on the topology, number of terminals, weight magnitudes, or ratio between positive weights.

A feasible solution is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that the graph on vertex set
\[
W=R\cup\bigcup_{\{u,v\}\in F}\{u,v\}
\]
with edge set \(F\) is connected and has no cycle. Thus the output is one tree containing all terminals; its other vertices may be any subset of the available nonterminals. Its cost and the optimum are
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(F)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=
\min\{\operatorname{cost}_I(F):F\text{ is a feasible solution of }I\}.
\]
Every valid instance has a feasible solution, so the minimum is over a nonempty finite set and is attained. Output edges must be original input edges. Neither new Steiner points outside \([n]\), a separate cost for selected vertices, a set of pairwise connection demands, nor directed edges are part of this problem.

The following encoding fixes the full bit cost. Write each weight uniquely as \(p_e/q_e\), where \(p_e\ge0\), \(q_e\ge1\), and the integers are relatively prime, so a zero weight is encoded as \(0/1\). Order edges lexicographically by their endpoints \(u<v\), obtaining \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), and order terminal labels increasingly, obtaining \(r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Form one list of integers consisting of \(n\), the explicit vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), \(m\), the four entries \(u,v,p_{e_j},q_{e_j}\) for each edge \(e_j=\{u,v\}\) in order, then \(h,r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Encode each integer in ordinary binary without leading zeros, with \(0\) represented by one zero. Put a separator \(\#\) between consecutive integers and no trailing separator. Finally encode the three symbols by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). The length of the resulting binary string is \(L(I)\). A valid output is the list consisting of \(|F|\) followed by the strictly increasing indices of the selected edges in \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), using the same integer, separator and binary-symbol encoding. All numerator, denominator, endpoint and output bits count; arithmetic on rational numbers is not a unit-cost operation.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and a sequential output tape. The input is delimited by end markers. Each transition reads the scanned symbols, can write one symbol per writable tape, and moves each head by at most one cell; it counts as one step. A transition may additionally read at most one fresh independent fair random bit. The program and tape count do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-arithmetic instruction or uncharged preprocessing. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the random bits.

The set \(\mathcal A\) contains exactly the machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input \(z\) and every random sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) steps, and on every valid instance and every such sequence its output encodes a feasible solution. Invalid inputs may receive any output within that same bound. The constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\), but not on the instance or the random bits. This is a bound on every execution, not merely an expected-time bound.

The random sequence \(\omega\) has the product distribution of independent fair bits; there is no probability distribution on inputs. Since at most \(C(L(I)+1)^k\) bits can be read, the expected cost is the finite average over all bit strings of that length, each with equal probability, disregarding unused bits. Infeasibility has no permitted error probability. The multiplicative bound must hold on every valid instance, with no additive cost term or exception for small inputs. Instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\) are included: their expected output cost must be zero. As every finite random execution has positive probability and costs are nonnegative, this requires zero output cost on every execution of such an instance.

Known polynomial-time approximations make \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}\) nonempty; it is bounded below by \(1\), so its infimum is a finite real number. An algorithm attaining exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=1\) would mean that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm achieves ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring an exact algorithm or one program that takes \(\varepsilon\) as an additional input.

For the conditional results in the context, \(\mathrm P\) is the class of languages decidable by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length binary certificates checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The class \(\mathrm{RP}\) consists of languages decided by randomized machines with polynomial running time on every random tape that never accept a no-instance and accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). No equality or separation among these classes is assumed in \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\).

context_blocks.text: The source model is an undirected weighted graph with a terminal subset; passing to shortest-path distances preserves the approximation problem. This card retains the canonical graph input with nonnegative rational weights, explicit binary encoding, worst-case polynomial time and expected feasible-output cost. These machine and encoding conventions make the inherited numerical target precise.

Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoß and Sanità obtain a polynomial-time \((\ln 4+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and their full account derandomizes the algorithm. Consequently the infimum satisfies the unconditional bounds \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le\ln 4\), without an assertion that the upper endpoint is attained.

Traub and Zenklusen obtain the same limiting guarantee by a combinatorial algorithm, first presented in their 2021 preprint and SODA 2022 paper and incorporated into their 2025 journal article. Their model discussion explicitly explains the compatibility of positive and nonnegative edge weights.

Chlebík and Chlebíková prove NP-hardness of achieving factors below \(96/95\). For the always-feasible randomized expected-cost model of this card, their gap reduction excludes those factors assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\); that randomized-model consequence is an editorial inference, not an unconditional lower bound.
The 2024 result bounding the bidirected cut relaxation's integrality gap by \(1.9988\) settles a different question about a specified relaxation.

A July 2026 primary paper still reports \(\ln 4+\varepsilon\) as the best known general Steiner Tree approximation guarantee. The checked bounds do not determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\).

why: Steiner Tree is a basic network-design problem and a recurring subproblem in more general connectivity objectives. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would establish how closely polynomial-time algorithms can approach optimal connection cost in unrestricted weighted graphs. The target compares all algorithms, making it broader than the accuracy of one method or the strength of one relaxation.

answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}
\]
for precisely the instance class and machine model above. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with
\[
\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u,\qquad u-\ell\le\frac1{50}
\]
qualifies through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The value need not be an integer, rational number or decimal expansion; exact determination is welcome but is not required. Merely renaming the defining infimum does not specify an answer.

The proof must respect the infimum's endpoint convention. To establish an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u\), achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above suffice; an algorithm achieving \(u\) itself is not required. Equivalently, one may prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an eligible algorithm whose expected cost on every instance is at most \((u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). A lower bound \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) must exclude every eligible algorithm from achieving each ratio \(r\) with \(1\le r<\ell\). For every such \(r\) and algorithm, this requires some valid instance with expected cost strictly greater than \(r\operatorname{OPT}\).

A hardness bound under an unproved complexity assumption proves only the corresponding conditional statement. It does not by itself certify the unconditional constant requested here. A gap for a particular linear-programming relaxation, the worst case of one selected algorithm, a guarantee only for a restricted graph family, or computations on finitely many input sizes do not determine this infimum over all eligible algorithms and all valid instances.
status_note: The inspected primary results give ratios approaching the natural logarithm of four and conditional inapproximability, leaving the optimal numerical constant undetermined. A bounded review through 16 September 2026 found no verified value or certified interval meeting this card's absolute error tolerance of one hundredth. The July 2026 primary literature still reports the natural logarithm of four plus arbitrarily small positive slack as the best known general Steiner Tree guarantee. The check distinguishes randomized expected cost from expected running time, NP-hardness from unconditional lower bounds, and integrality gaps and Steiner Forest results from this target. Definitions and theorem scopes were read in actual primary PDFs; the 2025 joint journal article was checked through its publication record and earlier primary preprint because direct PDF retrieval failed. This is not an exhaustive search, independent verification of all cited proofs, or an existing Lean verification.

sentences: Steiner Tree seeks a minimum-cost tree connecting a specified terminal set in an arbitrary undirected graph with nonnegative rational edge weights.
The target is the infimum of approximation ratios achieved by uniform randomized algorithms that always output a feasible tree and run in polynomial time on every random tape.
Each ratio bounds expected output cost on every instance, including those with zero optimum, while the algorithm may depend on the chosen ratio.
Known algorithms approach \(\ln 4\), but the checked hardness bounds are conditional and the bounded later review found no determination of the optimal constant at the requested precision.
An accepted answer supplies a real value with a complete Lean proof of absolute error at most \(1/100\), or a certified containing interval of width at most \(1/50\).

The original source permits metric closure on the same vertex set, with distances equal to shortest-path costs. The canonical general graph formulation is preserved. For rational input, shortest-path distances have polynomial-size rational encodings; a metric solution can be expanded into original paths and made a tree without increasing cost, while any original solution gives a metric solution no more expensive. This conventional equivalence is recorded as a model check, not a requirement to supply or use such a transformation in a solution.

Downloaded and read the actual Chlebik–Chlebikova author revision dated23May2008 from the Portsmouth institutional repository. Publisher and institutional metadata give TCS406(3):207–214,31Oct2008; inspected version is15pages. Read Theorem13 and its proof pp10–11: epsilon,k and one finite good expanderD are fixed constants before reducing an arbitrary input, so the proof establishes existence of a uniform deterministic polynomial-time gap reduction despite not constructively finding the expander family. Theorem14p11 in fact states a numerical factor1.01063>96/95; the public text uses the conservative exact96/95 and does not call it the strongest possible hardness number. The fixed weights can be chosen rational with slack in the strict parameter inequalities.

Randomized-model inference audited separately: for an eligible expected-ratio r<96/95 choose a fixed deterministic reduction gap with yes OPT<=B and no OPT>=bB, where r<b<96/95. Expected cost at most rB in a yes instance gives positive constant probability at least1-r/b of a feasible output costing<bB; a no-instance never produces such an output because all outputs are feasible. Constant independent repetitions give a one-sided polynomial-time decision algorithm for the NP-hard source language. Consequently the algorithm would imply NP=RP; under NP!=RP no such r is achievable, hence rho_ST>=96/95. This is an editorial consequence of the inspected gap reduction, not an unconditional lower bound or the literal randomized statement of the paper. P!=NP alone was not used to exclude randomized algorithms.

Tolerance audit: known unconditional1<=rho_ST<=ln4 has width about0.386, much larger than1/50. Even the checked conditional96/95lower bound would leave a gap much larger than1/50, and the assumption cannot certify the requested unconditional constant. Do not claim that1/100accuracy necessarily separates P from NP or NP from RP: that would require a separate argument, and the intervals around known nearby conditional possibilities can overlap.

The bit-model conventions are an explicit refinement of the existing benchmark definition. An algorithm has fixed finite code and one polynomial clock valid on all bit strings and all tapes; validating the explicit input promise can be done in polynomial bit time, so allowing arbitrary output on malformed inputs does not impose a different substantive Steiner Tree problem. The expectation is a finite rational average for each valid input; no exact real sampling primitive is assumed. Deterministic known upper-bound algorithms belong to this randomized class without random-sampling implementation issues.

The public target contains no recommended algorithm, lower-bound method, gap construction or intermediate milestone. It asks for one unconditional real constant within the recorded tolerance. The answer criterion handles nonattainment, algorithm-dependent polynomials, lower bounds over all eligible algorithms, all instances and zero optimum. No canonical file, queue state, selection, comment or publication was modified by this draft.
